transcript:
Meeting header:
- Date/Time: 2028-05-12 16:00 UTC
- Duration: 48 minutes
- Attendees: Alex Park (Redwood AE), Samira Khan (Redwood SE), Jordan Reed (LumenForge Lead ML Eng), Maya Lin (LumenForge Infra Lead), Carlos Vega (LumenForge CTO)

Auto-generated Summary:
LumenForge is evaluating options for hosting inference for their streaming, multi-turn user assistant. Primary concerns: p95 latency <= 220ms for short streaming responses, ability to sustain 250 concurrent streams with spikes up to 600 for 10s bursts, and cost tradeoffs between Redwood Hosted, Dedicated, and a VPC Private deployment. They asked for practical token/sec benchmarks, examples of batching/kv cache impact, and a checklist for private deployment network requirements.

Topics: Hosted vs Dedicated cost tradeoffs; p95 latency targets and measurement methodology; concurrency and token/sec benchmarking; streaming token bursts and fallback policies; KV cache and prefix caching; security requirements for private deployment (SSO/KMS/audit logs).

Transcript body:
[00:00] Alex (AE): hey everyone, thanks for joining, i think we have about 45 minutes, um, quick intros — i'm alex from redwood, samira is our systems SE, and then over to you all for quick intros
[00:12] Jordan (Customer): yeah i'm jordan, lead ml eng for lumenforge, we own the model infra and the assistant stack
[00:18] Maya (Customer): maya, infra lead, network and onprem connectivity
[00:22] Carlos (Customer): carlos, cto, just here for context and high level constraints
[00:27] Samira (SE): great, thanks. objective for today: understand your p95 targets, concurrency profile, and whether hosted/dedicated/private makes sense. we'll also try to give an initial test plan for token/sec streaming benchmarks
[00:40] Jordan: perfect. short background — our assistant supports streaming long answers, often with tool calls. typical short reply path is ~40-150 tokens; long replies up to 1.2k tokens. most critical is the short reply p95 because it's in the UI flow
[00:53] Alex: useful. what's your current p95 for short replies in your baseline?
[00:58] Jordan: on our infra we're hitting roughly 300-350 ms p95 right now, sometimes 420 on spikes, would like to get to <220 ms p95 with headroom
[01:10] Maya: and concurrency — we normally run 200-300 concurrent interactive streams, but marketing pushes cause bursts to 600+ for 10-30s windows, so we need graceful degradation
[01:23] Samira: ok makes sense. a couple clarifying q's: do you prioritize hard latency SLOs over cost or are you looking for a compromise?
[01:30] Carlos: latency is primary for user experience on the short path; cost matters but we'll pay for dedicated if it guarantees p95 and capacity isolation
[01:38] Alex: good, so likely a Dedicated or Private route but we should validate Hosted feasibility with our burst model and fallback policies. quick note — our runtime uses continuous batching and kv cache to improve throughput, does your stack use KV caching for repeated context?
[01:53] Jordan: yes we have prefix reuse across turns, we keep a short KV cache so repeated prompts are cheap, though we still see token generation cost for the live stream
[02:02] Samira: ok, for benchmarks we recommend separating two paths: short-response microbenchmarks (50 tokens, targeted p95) and long-response streaming throughput (tokens/sec sustained). we'll provide a harness that simulates tail bursts and concurrent open streams
[02:18] Jordan: can you share realistic numbers for token/sec per GPU and p95 expectations for hosted vs dedicated? i mean ballpark numbers to justify the procurement ask
[02:26] Alex: sure, and caveats — numbers vary by model family, sequence length, quantization, and GPU gen. for a typical Llama2-13B-ish variant, on current gen A100/H100 family, a well-tuned Dedicated pool with batching + kv cache can sustain ~12-18k tokens/sec per GPU for streaming workloads with single-digit-ms token generation increments; p95 short-reply latencies we often see in the 140-220ms range with proper batching and prefetching. Hosted endpoints may be slightly higher p95 due to multi-tenant scheduling, maybe +20-40 ms, but with fallbacks and reserved capacity we can tighten that
[03:03] Maya: what's the impact of batching on p95 for short replies? sounds like batching improves throughput but hurts tail latency
[03:10] Samira: correct, batching helps tokens/sec but increases head-of-line latency if you wait to batch. our runtime supports adaptive micro-batching where we do continuous flushing for low latency and larger batches when throughput allows. the idea is to set a per-route latency target and the runtime chooses batch windows to meet it
[03:29] Jordan: and kv cache — if the prefix is cached, how much does that shave off?
[03:33] Samira: depends on prefix length; for small prefixes that avoid early layers recompute, you might see 20-60% lower compute per token and decreased p95, especially for repeated short-turn replies. but cache hit rates matter — the harness should include cache-hit and miss scenarios
[03:46] Alex: for bursts — how do we handle 600 concurrent streams? do we need many GPUs or can we rely on autoscaling?
[03:53] Samira: Dedicated pools give predictable throughput and quicker scaling; hosted can autoscale but cold provisioning for GPUs causes temporary latency increases. for tight p95 SLOs, dedicated reserved capacity or private deployment with warm nodes is recommended. also we suggest a fast fallback policy — if you hit capacity, route to a smaller, cheaper model with graceful degradation for non-critical streams
[04:12] Carlos: any security differences for private vs dedicated? we have compliance constraints so audit logs and KMS integration are musts
[04:18] Alex: both Dedicated and Private support KMS/HSM integrations and audit logs. Private (VPC or on-prem) gives you control plane isolation and network-level controls; Dedicated provides isolation at cluster level but control plane is still managed — we can discuss SOC2 timelines and support docs after this call
[04:32] Jordan: ok, i'd like a practical benchmarking plan. can you outline what you'd like us to run and what you'll run on your side?
[04:37] Samira: we'll share a harness (Jenkins/Github actions friendly) that does: 1) short-response p95 microbench (50 tokens) at increasing concurrency; 2) sustained tokens/sec tests for long streams (1k+ tokens) measuring throughput per GPU; 3) burst test where concurrency steps from baseline to peak for 30s windows; 4) cache-hit vs miss matrix. we'll provide sample configs and a collection of synthetic payloads that approximate your traces
[04:58] Jordan: great. when you say tokens/sec per GPU, how do you measure tokenization and detokenization overhead? we do detokenization on the client usually
[05:05] Samira: we measure end-to-end server token emit rate at the runtime boundary including generation compute and any LM tokenizer that runs server-side. if you detokenize on the client, we'll adapt the harness; important thing is to measure server-side token production rate and client-observed latency for the first byte and p95 complete answer
[05:22] Maya: question about network egress and throughput for private deployments — what's the recommended network fabric?
[05:27] Alex: for on-prem or VPC, we recommend 25-100 Gbps interconnects between serving nodes and a low-latency fabric; we also provide a checklist for firewall rules and NAT traversal. we'll send the full network profile in the follow-up
[05:40] Jordan: any gotchas with model quantization for streaming? we've experimented with 4-bit quantization but saw some tail-quality issues
[05:46] Samira: quantization lowers memory and increases throughput but can worsen response quality for some prompts; we suggest hybrid approach — quantize for cold-start heavy models but run A/B checks and quality evals on production prompts. Redwood Optimize can suggest quantization profiles given your eval set
[05:58] Carlos: curious about cost math — what's the typical cost delta between Hosted and Dedicated for our scale? rough percent ballpark ok
[06:04] Alex: ballpark: Hosted is often 10-40% higher per-token than dedicated committed capacity at scale, because hosted absorbs multi-tenant overhead and burst provisioning. if you commit to dedicated capacity you get discounts and predictable unit economics; private has higher fixed lift but can be cheaper per-token at very large scale once amortized
[06:22] Jordan: what about cold-start from network/redis cache misses? we see random spikes when a user's session is routed to a cold node
[06:28] Samira: we recommend warm pools and prefix/KV caching pinned to sessions when possible; also sticky routing and session affinity reduce cold-starts. for hosted we offer session-affinity knobs for enterprise customers
[06:41] Alex: quick note to record — we'll produce two sets of numbers: an optimistic tokens/sec per-GPU assuming high cache-hit and batching, and a conservative set assuming 20-40% cache misses and micro-batching for latency
[06:55] Jordan: ok would be useful. for the test harness, can you give an example synthetic config that mimics our flows? we can then run internal validation before sharing traces
[07:02] Samira: yes, will include a config: baseline 250 concurrent streams, short-path p95 target 220ms, burst to 600 for 30s every 15 minutes, long-streams 50 concurrent with 1k token avg. we'll attach a yaml and a small node/python client to reproduce streaming semantics
[07:19] Maya: on network side, we'll need an explicit list of ports and domains to open for the private control plane and telemetry egress
[07:25] Alex: noted, we'll include that in the private deployment checklist and include sample firewall rules.
[07:33] Jordan: do you provide any tooling for inspecting per-token latency distribution or per-request traces?
[07:38] Samira: yes, Redwood Console exposes token-level timing breakdowns and per-request trace windows with KV-cache hit metadata — useful for diagnosing token stalls and hotspotting slow layers
[07:49] Carlos: what's the SLA for Dedicated? we need 99.9 something?
[07:54] Alex: Dedicated has an SLA tier we can back with uptime and latency SLOs per contract; 99.9% and specific p95 latency targets can be in the contract for committed pools. we'll surface the SLA doc in follow up
[08:06] Jordan: any suggestions for quick wins to improve our current 300ms p95 before we move to another infra? maybe software-level tweaks
[08:13] Samira: yes — frontload the KV cache, reduce tokenization on the server, enable micro-batching, profile model internals to find decoding bottlenecks, and ensure session affinity to avoid cold starting models. small engineering changes often yield 20-40% p95 improvement
[08:28] Alex: also look into route-based controls: classify short replies on a low-latency route and long replies on a throughput-first route, that way tuning is per-path
[08:36] Jordan: good idea.
[08:39] Maya: curious about fallback model variants — you mentioned smaller models for overflow, how transparent is that for the app?
[08:45] Samira: we've got automatic fallback policies that tag responses as degraded and include metadata so the app can opt to show reduced fidelity or queue user requests. fallback is seamless and policy-driven
[08:55] Jordan: ok this is helpful. last thing — do you run any independent benchmarks or can we run a joint benchmark where Redwood runs on your infra and we run ours and compare?
[09:03] Alex: we can run joint benchmarks; we'll run controlled runs on hosted/dedicated and share raw logs. recommend a 2-phase approach: 1) synthetic runs to validate baseline numbers; 2) run with a sample of your recorded traces (anonymized) to validate real-world behavior
[09:20] Carlos: sounds good. timeline-wise we'd like results to align with our budget cycle in mid-June
[09:26] Alex: alright we'll aim for initial numbers + pricing before 2028-05-24 so you can plan POs; deliverables are in next-steps
[09:34] Jordan: anything else?
[09:36] Samira: we'll also include a suggested A/B plan for quantization and model-size fallbacks with clear metrics to watch (latency, quality regression, token/sec)
[09:46] Alex: great. we'll follow up with docs. thanks everyone.
